title: Basketball Lexicon
intro: Rules (violations, fouls, game structure) have a single authority: the FIBA, NBA and NCAA rulebooks. Where the three differ, the entry gives each value.

Actions, sets, systems and coverages have no governing body. Names vary by team, coach and country. Each definition states what the sources agree on; regional or team-specific meanings are flagged as variants, not merged.
Analytics follow the NBA.com and Basketball-Reference glossaries and Dean Oliver's definitions.
Slang and history are cross-checked against at least one glossary or dictionary plus a primary or press source where one exists.
Where sources conflict, the conflict is stated, not resolved by guesswork. Terms with several meanings are collected again in Disputed and multi-meaning terms.
Player numbers follow the usual convention: 1 point guard, 2 shooting guard, 3 small forward, 4 power forward, 5 center.

sections.title: Court areas and spots
sections.note: The names coaches use for places on the floor. Rulebook measurements are given where a rule depends on them.

entries.definition: Boundary line at each end of the court, behind the basket.
Boundary line along each long side of the court.

entries.aka: Center line, midcourt line; "10-second line" in NCAA and high school
entries.definition: Divides the court into frontcourt and backcourt. In the NBA the line itself belongs to the backcourt.
The half containing the basket a team attacks. Second meaning: a team's forwards and center.
The half a team defends. Second meaning: a team's guards.

Rectangle from the baseline to the free-throw line. Width: FIBA 4.90 m (edges 2.45 m from the endline midpoint), NBA 16 ft, NCAA men 12 ft. "Key" usually means the lane plus the free-throw circle. FIBA's rulebook calls this rectangle the "restricted area" (see Disputed terms).

entries.aka: Charge circle, block-charge arc; FIBA: no-charge semicircle
entries.definition: Arc under the basket. A secondary defender standing inside it cannot draw a charge on an airborne shooter or passer. NBA radius 4 ft from the center of the ring; FIBA about 1.3 m.
The painted box or mark on each side of the lane near the baseline, and the low-post spot next to it.
Area beside the lane near the basket, around the block.
Area along the free-throw line, including both elbows.
Where the free-throw line meets the lane line. A common catch and mid-range spot.
The elbow area, usually on the weak side, used as a passing hub in Princeton and Triangle actions.
The middle of the free-throw line. Also the help spot a defender takes there.
Baseline area between the block and the corner, about 12 ft from the basket. A key spot against zones.
Baseline area just outside the lane near the backboard, where bigs wait for dump-offs and offensive rebounds.
Area outside the lane on either side, around the free-throw line extended. Also a player type (2 or 3).
Spot on the arc between the top of the key and the wing.
Area above the free-throw circle, straight out from the basket. "Point" names the spot out front.
Where the baseline meets the sideline. The corner three is the shortest three: NBA 22 ft, FIBA 6.60 m.

FIBA: 6.75 m arc, 6.60 m in the corners (straight lines 0.90 m from the sidelines). NBA: 23 ft 9 in arc, 22 ft in the corners (lines 3 ft from the sidelines). NCAA men and women: 22 ft 1¾ in, the FIBA distance, men since 2019-20 and women since 2021-22.
Line the shooter stands behind on a free throw. NBA: 15 ft from the face of the backboard. FIBA: 5.80 m from the inner edge of the endline.
Circle at midcourt where the opening jump ball is taken.

NBA sideline marks 28 ft from the baseline: the frontcourt throw-in spot after a timeout in the last two minutes. NCAA men (2025-26) also use 28-ft marks for frontcourt throw-ins above the free-throw line extended.
FIBA frontcourt line opposite the scorer's table. Used after a late-game timeout (coach's choice) and after unsportsmanlike or disqualifying fouls.
The center-court logo. A "logo three" is shot from near it.
Area outside the paint but inside the three-point line.
The half of the floor, split lengthwise, where the ball is.
The half of the floor away from the ball, where help defenders sit.
The space between the ball handler and the nearest perimeter teammate. Defenders "play the gap" to stop drives.

sections.title: Positions and player roles
sections.note: The five numbered positions are still the shared language, but sources agree they have blurred since the 1980s Lakers, the 1990s Bulls, the 2010s Heat and the Warriors' small-ball era.

entries.definition: Main ball handler and passer. Runs the offense and sets up teammates. Traditionally the shortest player.
Perimeter scorer who shoots from three and long mid-range, gets open off the ball and spaces the floor.
The most versatile spot: scores, rebounds, handles, passes and defends on the wing.
Stronger forward who scores near the basket and mid-range, rebounds and defends inside. Modern 4s are often expected to shoot threes.
Usually the tallest player. Plays near the basket: rebounds, protects the rim, sets screens.
Perimeter player who usually plays away from the basket (1 or 2).
Player at the 3 or 4, responsible for scoring and rebounding.

entries.aka: Big man, big woman, post player
entries.definition: Physically large post player, usually a 4 or 5.
Player who can play either the 2 or the 3 and works on the wings.
Guard who plays both point guard and shooting guard.
Forward with traits of both a small forward and a power forward.
Forward with point-guard passing and handling who runs the offense. Examples cited: Scottie Pippen (Bulls), LeBron James (Heat).
Power forward who shoots from outside, pulling a defender out of the paint. Useful as a pick-and-pop screener.
Center who shoots from the perimeter.
Player between two positions who is not ideal at either.
Role player whose value is three-point shooting and perimeter defense.
Shot-blocking big who guards the paint.
Big who sprints to the rim in transition to beat his defender for a quick score.
The last big up the floor in transition, who settles near the top of the key.
Perimeter scorer who mainly attacks by driving to the basket.
The first and most important player off the bench.
Non-star who contributes a specific skill: shooting, defense or rebounding.
Approach where players cover several traditional positions, valuing versatility, ball skills, shooting and switching.
Lineup with smaller, quicker players, often a forward playing center. The Warriors' "Death Lineup" (Draymond Green at center) is the reference example.

sections.title: Individual skills and moves
sections.note: Footwork, ball handling, shooting, post play, passing and individual defense. Where a move touches the travelling rule, the rule entry is in Rules.

entries.definition: Stance after the catch, ready to shoot, pass or dribble.
Quick step at the defender with the non-pivot foot to set up a drive or shot.
Stepping with one foot while the other, the pivot foot, stays on the floor. Front pivot steps forward; reverse pivot steps backward.
Ending a dribble or catch by landing on both feet at once; either foot can then pivot. NCAA women's rules (2025-26) state it is legal when the feet land at about the same time.
Stop where the feet land one after the other; the first foot down becomes the pivot foot.
The moment a player gains enough control to hold, pass or shoot the ball. The NBA rulebook defines it; the step count starts after it.

Popular name for the step taken while gathering, before the two legal steps. Neither rulebook uses the phrase: FIBA and the NBA both count "step one" from the first foot down after control is gained, which has the same effect.
Shooting footwork with two steps into the shot (a right-hander steps left, then right).
After picking up the dribble, a step one way then a second step the other way to get past a defender. Credited to Šarūnas Marčiulionis in the NBA (1989), popularized by Manu Ginóbili in the 2000s.
A small hop into a two-foot landing before a shot. Different from the illegal "hop" in NBA rules: landing on the same foot twice in a row when ending a dribble.
Dribble moved from one hand to the other in front of the body to change direction.
Dribble pulled toward the body then pushed back out with the same hand, faking a crossover.
Switching hands by bouncing the ball behind the back.
A full reverse pivot while dribbling to roll past a defender.
Slowing down, then exploding past the defender.
Dribbling backward to escape pressure or create space.
Hard dribble aimed at beating the defender, not just moving the ball.
After using a ball screen, weaving back toward the side the dribbler started from.
Crossover where the ball is pushed out with one hand and pulled back with the other. Named after God Shammgod; former Yugoslav players used it earlier.
Sweeping the ball across the body from triple threat, low or high, to protect it and open a drive or pass.
Faking a shot with the feet planted to get the defender off the floor.
Faking a pass to move the defender before passing elsewhere.
Shot released while in the air.
Shot taken with the feet planted, without jumping. The standard shot before the jump shot spread.
Jump shot taken off the dribble.
Stepping away from the defender to create space before shooting, often for a three.
Jump shot taken while drifting backward away from the basket.
High-arcing shot released early, usually by a smaller player, to clear taller defenders.
Close shot, usually banked off the backboard.
Layup rolled off the fingertips with a high arc.
Layup finished on the far side of the rim after going under it.
Shot that bounces off the backboard into the basket.
One-handed shot taken sideways to the basket, the arm swinging over the head.
Kareem Abdul-Jabbar's very high, long-range hook. Name coined by Bucks broadcaster Eddie Doucette.
Shorter hook. Magic Johnson's name for his version (1987 Finals).
Hook taken off two feet; more balanced and quicker, but lower.
Putting the ball directly through the hoop with one or both hands.
Pass near the rim caught in the air and scored in one motion, often a dunk.
Scoring immediately after an offensive rebound.
Underhand shot, famously Rick Barry's free throw.
Taking position near the basket with the back to it to receive the ball.
Using the body to pin a defender behind you to receive a pass.
Post move: stepping into the lane and sealing the defender with the inside foot.
Turning to face the basket after the catch.
Post move: stepping back past the defender with the baseline or middle foot toward the basket.
Post move: shot fake, then step through under the jumping defender.
Hakeem Olajuwon's series of post fakes and spins, which he said he adapted from soccer.
Dribbling backward from the perimeter into the low post to post up.
Two-handed pass from the chest to a teammate's chest.
Pass that hits the floor once before reaching the receiver.
Two-handed pass thrown from above the head.
Long one-handed overhead throw.
Pass across the floor that skips one or more teammates.
The pass that starts a set, often into the post.
Rebounder's first pass to start a fast break.
Long pass up the floor to start a quick attack.
Pass from the paint out to a shooter beyond the arc.
Pass through a small gap, often to the roller in a pick-and-roll.
High pass over a defender, often to a fronted post player.
Short underhand pass in tight space.
Pass thrown without looking at the target.
Pass thrown around a defender's body.
Short pass in the paint for an easy score.
Athletic stance: knees bent, arms out, weight balanced.
Defensive footwork: lead foot steps toward the opponent, trail foot slides after it.
Running at a shooter or receiver under control to contest or contain.
Getting a hand up close enough to affect a shot. NBA tracking counts a contest when the nearest defender is within 3.5 ft.
Getting a hand on the ball on a non-shot.
Taking possession by intercepting a pass or knocking the ball from a dribbler.
Chasing defender knocking the ball away from behind the dribbler.
Deflecting a shot so it misses.
Defender establishing a legal position so the offensive player who runs into him is called for an offensive foul.

sections.title: Screens and cuts
sections.note: Screens are named by the direction they send the cutter. The Basketball Action Dictionary groups off-ball screens into four families: down (baseline to top), back (toward the basket), cross (across toward the ball) and flare (away from the ball). Most named screens below are one of these at a specific spot.

entries.definition: Legal block by a stationary player that delays a defender from reaching a spot. A moving screen is an offensive foul.
Screen set on the defender of the player with the ball. Basis of the pick-and-roll.
Screen set for a player without the ball.
Screener moves toward the baseline and screens so the cutter comes up toward the ball or the top.
Screen set on a defender's back so the cutter goes toward the basket. Wikipedia narrows it to a post player screening for a perimeter teammate; coaching sources use it for any screen toward the rim.
Screen set by a player moving up from a lower spot; in practice a back screen set from below.
Screen that sends the cutter horizontally across the lane, often to free a post player.
Screen that sends a shooter away from the ball along the arc.
Baseline cross screen near the weak-side block for a player cutting from the far corner into the lane. Core of the Flex offense.
Back screen at the high post for a guard who passed to the wing and cuts to the basket (the UCLA cut).
Back screen, traditionally a guard screening for a big.
Angled back screen by a guard for a big cutting to the low block.
Back screen from the weak-side slot for a cutter to the basket; part of the Princeton "Chin" series.
Back screen for a wing.
Baseline screen near the dunker spot that sends a cutter to the corner.
Low screen facing the basket that frees a corner or wing player.
Down screen for a player cutting from the block straight up the lane to the slot or top.
Two screens in a row, in the same direction, for one cutter.
Two screeners side by side for one cutter.
Two screeners stand apart; the shooter runs between them and they close together behind him.
A player sets a screen, then immediately receives a screen from a teammate.
Screen set behind a defender who cannot see it.
Cut that rubs past a defender without a set screen, so it stays legal.
Ball screen set at a diagonal to push the defender into a bad spot or direct the dribbler.
Ball screen with the screener facing half court, so the dribbler can go either way.
Side ball screen with the screener's back parallel to the baseline, set from below.
The screener runs at a screen but never sets it and pops or cuts into space.
The screener cuts to the basket early instead of finishing the screen.
Player who looks set to ball-screen instead sets an off-ball screen, often a wide pin-down.
Offensive player screens his own defender to stop a switch.
Slang: a screen that walls off the screener's own defender to clear a driving lane, often illegal.
Screen where the screener moves into the defender or does not give the required distance. Offensive foul.
Any quick off-ball move to get open.
Cut straight toward the basket.
Cut behind an overplaying defender toward the basket.
Basket cut in front of the defender, the opposite of a back cut.
Move toward the defender, then break sharply out to receive a pass.
Cut up the lane, then out to the wing, shaped like an L.
Coming off a screen and turning tightly back toward the basket.
Wide curved cut instead of a straight one.
Unscreened cut toward the ball, often into the high post.
Cut from the top past a high-post back screen to the low post.
The cut off the shuffle (slice) screen in the Shuffle offense.
Angled cut from the wing toward the basket.
Wing-to-wing cut across the top, usually off bigs at both elbows. Named after Allen Iverson, who ran it so often coaches adopted the name.
Basket cut by the player who just passed into the post.
After passing to the elbow big, the guard cuts off him to the rim.
Weak-side wing slides to the corner when the ball handler drives baseline.
Baseline cut from the weak side to the strong-side corner.
Corner player rises to the wing to open space, often for a roller.
Nearest perimeter player relocates to the spot a driver left.
Two teammates swap spots.
Pass, cut to the basket, take the return pass.
Pass, then follow the ball to set a ball screen or receive a handoff.
Catching on the move and driving without stopping to square up.
Declining a screen: the cutter goes backdoor, or the dribbler drives away from the ball screen.

sections.title: Named actions
sections.note: An action is a two- or three-player building block; a play strings actions together. These names are coaching shorthand, not rules, so the same action can carry different names on different teams. The biggest overlap is Chicago = Zoom: most sources treat them as one action.

entries.definition: A teammate screens the ball handler's defender, then rolls to the basket for a pass.
Ball screen where the screener steps out to the perimeter for a shot instead of rolling.
The roller stops around the free-throw line, catches and plays from there, often against traps.
The screener slips early into the open space near the elbow for a short roll; a counter to ice and blitz.
Ball screen set in transition before the defense is organized.
Two ball screens in a row in early offense, usually by two bigs; the second screener often screens for the first.
Double drag where the second screener screens the first screener back toward the ball.
Ball screen on the wing, often set from below as a step-up screen.
Middle ball screen with all three other players beyond the arc.
Spread pick-and-roll with the screen set near a slot, angled to send the dribbler middle (D'Antoni style) or toward the sideline.
Pick-and-roll with no offensive player in the corner on that side. Opposite: "filled corner".
A guard or wing sets the ball screen for a big.

Middle pick-and-roll in which a third player back-screens the roller's defender, then pops for a three. Coach's Clipboard credits Spain's national team; Hooper University names coach Sergio Scariolo and the 2016 Olympics.
The player who will set the ball screen first receives an off-ball screen (often a down screen), then runs into the pick-and-roll.
Right after a ball screen, the same screener turns and screens again the other way, often when the defender went under.
The screener switches the screen's angle at the last moment, so the dribbler goes the other way.
Two different players set ball screens in opposite directions, usually from Horns.
Ball screen near the nail for a big at the elbow, set by the other big; popularized by the Phoenix Suns.
Empty two-player wing ball screen; a double-drag variant in Pistol offense.
After the roller dives, a teammate fills the spot he left.
Side action: a player sets a wedge screen for a teammate who then sets the wing ball screen.
A cut or flash to the ball side to punish hedges or blitzes.
A player dribbles toward a teammate and hands him the ball as they pass, often screening his defender.
Pass to a teammate, then sprint to receive a handoff back from him.
Fake the handoff and keep the ball to attack.

A player comes off a pin-down screen straight into a dribble handoff. The Action Dictionary says Zak Boisvert named it after the Bulls running it for Derrick Rose; Ronsen Basketball and Coach Hoops treat Zoom as the same action.

Pin-down into a dribble handoff, usually with the handoff man rolling and a third player lifting. Breakthrough lists middle, staggered, back-screen and BLOB versions. One source (Action Dictionary index) uses Zoom more broadly for any screen-plus-DHO combo.

Early-offense three-player action started by the wing with the ball: pass-and-follow handoff or a wing screen for the ball handler. In Triangle language, "Pistol" can also mean the pin-down-into-DHO (Chicago).
Dribble handoff followed by a ball screen for the same player.
Rip (back) screen followed by a dribble handoff.
Flare screen followed by a handoff from the top big.
Cut up the middle of the lane before a handoff near the top.
A player flashes high, catches, and feeds a backdoor cutter.
Pass and immediate return pass, giving the original handler a live dribble against a moving defense.
High-post player passes to a low-post teammate near the rim.
A player coming off a screen turns and screens for the teammate who just screened for him.
A shooter starts under the basket and chooses a screen on either side, classically a single screen on one side and a double on the other.

While the ball handler drives baseline, a weak-side screen frees a shooter drifting to the far corner or wing. Grantland and Breakthrough describe the screen as a back screen; the Action Dictionary calls it a flare. Strongly associated with the Spurs.
Wing-to-wing cut across the top off bigs at both elbows, often to start Horns.
See Elevator screen: two screeners close the gap after a shooter runs through.
Princeton-style series from a high post: a back screen (chin screen), ball screens and flare screens.
UCLA screen for a non-point guard, followed by a side ball screen.
One elbow big cross-screens for the other, who cuts to the far wing.
After a post entry, two perimeter players screen for each other while the post reads them.
Drive draws help, then pass out to the open shooter.
Drive one way, then pass back to the spot the drive started from.
One player is given one side of the floor to go one-on-one.

sections.title: Sets and alignments
sections.note: A set is the starting formation; the actions above are what happens from it. Number names count players outside the arc first, then inside ("4-out 1-in").

entries.definition: Ball handler at the top, two bigs at the elbows, two players in the corners. Entry is usually a ball screen from either elbow or a pass to an elbow.
Ball handler at the top, both post players up at the elbows, the other two on the perimeter. Coach's Clipboard files it as the "stack offense"; the usual picture has the wings level with the elbows.
Both wings drop down to the corners.
One player up top, three across the free-throw line extended, one on the baseline; a common zone attack.
Three perimeter players and two post players.
Four perimeter players and one post player.
All five players start on the perimeter, leaving the lane empty for cuts and drives.
Generic term for spacing all non-screeners beyond the arc around one action, as in the spread pick-and-roll.
Fast 5-out early-offense look: ball handler on a wing, a guard in the strong-side corner, a big at the top.
Three players on the strong side, a weak-side big at the elbow, a forward near the slot.
5-out series started by passing to the trailing big at the top.
Uses the weak-side elbow big as a passing hub, with no defender between him and the sideline.
Four players at the corners of a rectangle around the lane; common on baseline out-of-bounds plays.
Players lined up close together in a column, used to score on baseline inbounds plays.
Putting more offensive players on one side than the defense has there, usually against a zone.
A team's base defensive alignment (also the drill that teaches it).

sections.title: Offensive systems, old and new
sections.note: A system is a whole-possession philosophy built from sets and actions. Origins are given only where a source states them; several systems have competing origin stories.

entries.definition: Free-flowing offense run by rules (pass away, screen away, cut) rather than a fixed pattern. Wikipedia credits Bob Knight, who built it at Army and Indiana, studied the passing game at the 1972 Olympic trials and refined it with Pete Newell. Variants are named by spacing: 4-out 1-in, 5-out.
Fixed pattern of passes and cuts that ends back in the starting formation, so it can repeat indefinitely (Flex, Shuffle, Swing).

Half-court system of constant movement, backdoor cuts, screens on and off the ball, and five players who can all pass, shoot and dribble. Earlier roots with Cappy Cappon and Red Sarachek; developed and popularized by Pete Carril at Princeton (1967-1996). NBA versions ran in Sacramento and elsewhere.

Built on a sideline triangle (post, wing, corner) with spacing that lets every player pass to the other four, the defense dictating each read. Basic ideas from Sam Barry at USC; developed by Tex Winter. Phil Jackson won 11 NBA titles with it: six with the Bulls, five with the Lakers.

Continuity offense built on the flex (baseline cross) screen followed by a down screen for the screener, repeated side to side. Wikipedia credits Rene Herrerias at Cal (1967). Gary Williams won the 2002 NCAA title with it at Maryland; Jerry Sloan ran a version with the Utah Jazz.

Continuity offense in which all five players rotate through five positions, built around the shuffle cut. Developed by Bruce Drake at Oklahoma in the early 1950s; used by Bob Spear at Air Force (1957-1971).
John Wooden's system built around a skilled high-post center, featuring the UCLA cut off a high-post back screen. Wooden adopted it on Press Maravich's advice before Lew Alcindor's varsity debut.
4-out continuity that alternates a UCLA screen with a slice or pin-down screen-the-screener.
Dick Bennett's offense that splits players into movers (scorers) and blockers (screeners).

entries.aka: DDM, AASAA, Memphis Attack, Walberg offense
entries.definition: Spreads the floor so a driver, usually the point guard, attacks the rim; help defenders leave shooters open. Created by Vance Walberg at Clovis West High School (1997); popularized by John Calipari at Memphis from 2005-06.
Offense where players react to what the ball handler does rather than running set plays.
4-out read-and-react offense blending Princeton and Triangle ideas, often started with a pass to the elbow big.

Stalling offense: four players in the half-court corners, one dribbling in the middle, to protect a lead. Developed by John McLendon by the early 1950s; popularized by Dean Smith at UNC in the early 1960s. Frustration with stalling helped push the NCAA to adopt a shot clock in 1985.

Mike D'Antoni's Phoenix Suns with Steve Nash (from 2004-05), who tried to shoot within the first seven seconds of the shot clock and led the NBA in pace, offensive rating and threes. Named after Jack McCallum's 2006 book on the 2005-06 season.
The modern NBA style descended from SSOL: push the pace, spread the floor, shoot many threes.
Don Nelson's unconventional style: quick, athletic players and heavy three-point shooting without a true center.
Push for early shots on offense and press full court on defense. Paul Westhead made it famous at Loyola Marymount in the early 1980s.
David Arseneault's extreme run-and-gun at Grinnell College (from 1989): heavy three-point volume, constant full-court pressure, and five-player line changes like hockey.
Roy Williams' 4-out transition offense with a rim runner, two wings, a ball handler and a trailing big.

Analytics-driven shot profile tied to Daryl Morey's Houston Rockets: threes (especially corner threes) and shots at the rim, avoiding long twos. In 2017-18 the Rockets took 82% of their shots as threes or restricted-area attempts.
Offense that revolves around one perimeter star who handles most possessions and creates his own shots, driving his usage rate up. The Ringer calls Michael Jordan the first heliocentric superstar.
Offense designed to attack zone defenses, typically by overloading, skip passes, short-corner and high-post touches.

sections.title: Transition and tempo
sections.note: Terms for the seconds after possession changes, on both ends.

entries.definition: Attacking right after gaining possession, before the defense is set. Synergy has no shot-clock cutoff: a possession is transition while the defense is not set.
Quick push up the floor for an easy score, often after a steal, block or rebound.
The second wave after the first break is stopped but before the defense is fully set; flows into the half-court offense.
Offense run once both teams are set.
Player who releases up the floor early, as the shot goes up, to get ahead of the defense. Synergy tags it as a transition role.
One player skipping defense to wait near the other basket for an easy score.
Short play designed for a shot within the first action.
Defense while the opponent is advancing after a change of possession, before both teams are set.
Coach's call to sprint back on defense after a shot.
When a shot goes up, the two defenders opposite the shooter sprint back to half court.
In transition, getting below the ball before matching up.
Two retreating defenders against a break: the top one stops the ball, the back one takes the first pass.
In transition, guarding the biggest threat first, not necessarily your own man.
Nearest defender pressures the outlet pass to slow the break.
In transition, the point guard pressures the inbound receiver to force a return pass.
Stretch where one team outscores the other by a wide margin ("a 12-0 run").
Late in a period, shooting early enough to get the ball back for a second shot before time expires.

sections.title: Man-to-man defense principles
sections.note: Positioning and help concepts used in any man defense. Teams use private call words (colors, codes) for many of these; the generic name comes first here.

entries.definition: Each defender is assigned one opponent.
Guarding the player with the ball.
Guarding players without the ball: denying, helping, recovering.
Maximum pressure on the ball handler.
Stay in front of the dribbler and keep him from penetrating.
Positioning in the passing lane to stop your man from catching.
Standing on the passing line between the ball and your man.
A step or two off the passing line toward the ball and basket, seeing both ball and man.
Perimeter defenders sag one or two steps into the gaps to stop drives.
Leaving your man briefly to stop penetration or protect the rim.
Defenders on the weak side sagging toward the lane to help.
A second rotation to cover the man left open by the first helper.
Leaving your man to stop the ball or protect the basket, with teammates shifting to cover.
Every defender shifts toward the ball on every pass.

entries.aka: Load to the ball, pack it in
entries.definition: Off-ball defenders collapse toward the ball to clog driving lanes.
Helper drops below the ball to pick up an offensive player or clog the lane.
Help defender steps into the lane to bump a roller or cutter, then recovers.
Weak-side help defender nearest the baseline and rim; usually rotates to the roller.
Defender at the nail who helps on drives up the middle.
The low man and the weak-side wing defender ("high I") together.
A fake toward a second player to slow him until a teammate recovers.
Help defender drops into the lane before the pass arrives to clog the paint.
A designated helper rotates early, before the action finishes.
Staying directly between the dribbler and the basket to stop penetration.
Pushing the dribbler toward the baseline. Philosophies conflict: the pack line never allows a baseline drive.
Two defenders on one offensive player.
Two defenders double the ball handler to force a turnover or bad pass, often on the sideline or in a corner.
Defending in front of the post player, between him and the ball, giving up a lob.
Defending the post from behind (one team's call word: Silver).
Perimeter defender drops down to slap at a post player's dribble, then recovers.
The low man doubles a post-up from the baseline side.
Sagging far off a non-shooter, daring him to shoot.
Center guards a non-shooting perimeter player and sags into the paint as a free rim protector.

Man defense from Dick Bennett (shown at UW-Green Bay, 1994; named with a 2005 DVD) and later Tony Bennett's Virginia. One defender pressures the ball; the other four stay inside an imaginary pack line to stop drives. Sources differ on the line: about 16 ft from the rim (SI, Basketball for Coaches) versus about 2 ft inside the three-point line (Wikipedia).
Drill for teaching help positions, rotations and closeouts.

sections.title: Screen coverages
sections.note: How two defenders handle a screen. For ball screens the coverage is mostly defined by where the screener's defender starts: deep (drop), level (at the level), high (hedge, blitz) or swapped (switch). Call words differ by team; Ice alone has at least four names.

entries.definition: Screener's defender sits below the screen, near the paint, and backpedals as the ball handler comes off; concedes pull-up jumpers to protect the rim.

entries.aka: Up to touch, catch, catch hedge
entries.definition: Screener's defender sits level with the screen, or one step below, to contain the ball handler until his teammate recovers.
Screener's defender starts just below the screen and steps out to contain, without fully committing.
Screener's defender jumps out hard at the ball handler to slow or redirect him, then recovers to the screener.
Screener's defender goes high and traps the ball handler with the on-ball defender. Some teams call an early trap before the screen "fire".
The two defenders swap assignments.

On a side ball screen, the on-ball defender jumps to the screen side and forces the ball handler toward the sideline, away from the screen; the big sits at or below the level of the screen on that side to meet him. Keeps the ball out of the middle.
On-ball defender forces the ball handler to his weak hand, away from the screen.
On-ball defender goes over the top of the screen, staying attached to the ball handler.
On-ball defender goes underneath the screen and the screener's defender; concedes the jumper to a non-shooter.
The nail defender switches onto the ball handler coming off the screen.
An off-ball switch before the ball screen, so a better defender ends up on the screener.
Switch, then double-team the mismatch.
Aggressive switch where the new defender jumps into the ball handler's path with contact.
A help defender switches onto a beaten ball handler; the original defender peels off to take the helper's man.
The tagging defender switches onto the roller or cutter; his original defender peels to the open man.
Off-ball switch that fixes a mismatch left by an earlier switch.
Tom Thibodeau's man/zone hybrid: helpers load to the ball side early.
Defender sits on the high side of the cutter to take away the screen, often forcing a backdoor cut instead.
Stay attached to the cutter's hip and follow him over the screen.
Lock onto the cutter, take him into the screen and ride over the top.
Stay attached, then decide whether to ride over the screen or cut through the gap to beat the cutter to the spot.
Bump the cutter into the screen, release and go under to meet him on the far side.
Slide through the gap between the screener and the teammate guarding him.
Push the cutter away from the ball into weak-side help.
Emergency switch: the beaten defender chases back to the cutter.
After an emergency switch, the mismatched defender fights to front or steal.
A big bumps a smaller teammate's matchup out to the perimeter to undo an inside mismatch.

sections.title: Zones, combination defenses and presses
sections.note: Zone names list defenders from the top of the floor to the baseline (2-3 = two up, three back). Press names follow the same order from the ball's end of the court.

entries.definition: Each defender guards an area and whoever enters it, not a specific opponent.
Two defenders up top, three along the baseline. The most common zone.
Three defenders across the top, one on each block.
One defender up top, three across the free-throw line, one under the rim; forces long passes and suits trapping.
One defender at the point, two at the elbows or wings, two low; played half or full court, with or without traps.
Zone in which each defender plays man-to-man on whoever is in his area.

Shape-shifting man/zone hybrid from a diamond look, built to confuse and force turnovers. Breakthrough ties it to Jerry Tarkanian's UNLV; Wikipedia credits Pitt assistant Fran Webster in the 1970s, with Tim Grgurich carrying it to UNLV.
Mix of zone and man aimed at one or two specific scorers.
Four defenders in a box zone; one plays man-to-man on the best scorer.
Like box-and-one, but the four zone players form a diamond.
Three defenders in a triangle zone; two play man-to-man on the two best scorers.
A zone shifting too far to one side, often forced by quick ball reversal.
Defensive pressure over the whole court, starting at the inbound pass; man or zone.
Full-court or three-quarter-court press played with zone principles and traps.
Offensive plan for advancing the ball against a press.
Diamond-shaped full-court zone press with a defender on the inbounder; tries to deflect the inbound or trap the first pass.
Three-quarter-court zone press that leaves the inbounder free, lets the first pass in, then traps once the ball handler commits.
Each defender picks up his man full court, pressuring rather than trapping.
Full-court man press in which a defender leaves his man to jump the dribbler (often from the blind side) and teammates rotate. Britannica credits Dean Smith.
Defense that waits near half court and traps as the ball crosses, often in the half-court corners.

Wikipedia's example: 40s are full-court man, 20s half-court man; the last digit sets the tactic (0 stay with your man, 1 trap the first pass, 2 trap the second pass, 3 fake the trap, 4 farthest player attacks the ball). Team-specific.
Two defenders trap the ball handler against the sideline.
Backcourt pressure aimed at forcing an 8-second violation.
Shaka Smart's full-court turnover-forcing system at VCU from 2009: mainly man-to-man traps, plus a 1-2-1-1 diamond and about 11 variations.
Nolan Richardson's full-court pressure and conditioning style at Arkansas; the offense was called "Hog Ball".
Gaining possession after a missed field goal or last free throw.
Rebound by the team that took the shot. In the NBA and FIBA it resets the shot clock to 14 if the ball hit the rim; in NCAA men's play, to 20.
Rebound by the defending team, ending the opponent's possession.
Getting between your opponent and the basket with body and arms to keep him off the ball.
Tapping a missed shot into the basket without catching it.
Foul for pushing or climbing on an opponent who already has rebounding position.
Holding a rebound tight under the chin, elbows out, to protect it.
Set play to inbound from the baseline under the basket being attacked.
Set play to inbound from the sideline.
Special play called coming out of a timeout.
Any set play to get the ball in from out of bounds, ideally for a quick score.
Pre-agreed counter that players run when the defense shows a specific coverage.

NBA: after a timeout in the last two minutes of the 4th quarter or overtime, the offense may throw in from the 28-ft frontcourt hash instead of the backcourt. FIBA: in the same window the head coach chooses a frontcourt throw-in line or the backcourt.
Deliberate foul to stop the clock or regain the ball, mostly late in a half or game.
Deliberate foul to stop a fast break. NBA (since 2022-23): one free throw by any player on the court plus possession, except in the last two minutes of the 4th quarter and overtime.
Early foul on a fast break by a defender to stop play. FIBA handles it under the unsportsmanlike foul criterion for unnecessary contact to stop a fast break.

Deliberately fouling a poor free-throw shooter. First used by Don Nelson's Mavericks on Dennis Rodman (1997); named for Shaquille O'Neal. Since 2016-17 the NBA penalizes away-from-the-play fouls in the last two minutes of every quarter.
Basket released just before time expires in a period.

Desperation end-of-period shot. NBA stat rule (approved Sept 2025): a shot from 36 ft or more in the last 3 seconds of the 1st, 2nd or 3rd quarter, on a play started in the backcourt, counts as a team attempt, not the player's.

sections.title: Rules
sections.note: Values reflect the FIBA Official Basketball Rules 2024, the NBA rulebook posted for 2026-27, and NCAA rules for 2025-26 and 2026-27 (2026-27 is not an NCAA rules-change year). FIBA rules govern international competition.

groups.title: FIBA vs NBA vs NCAA at a glance

entries.term: Shot clock after offensive rebound off the rim
values: Not confirmed in sources reviewed; 20 s after a frontcourt dead-ball throw-in (2025-26)
10 s (called at 19 on the shot clock, May 2026 change)
2 FTs from the 5th team foul per quarter (OT counts as Q4)
2 FTs from the 5th per quarter, the 4th in OT, or the 2nd in the last 2 min
1-and-1 from the 7th per half; 2 FTs from the 10th
1 FT, then play resumes with the team that had the ball (Art. 36.3.2)
2 FTs (Class A); 1 FT (Class B, per Basketball for Coaches, 2025)
5 s holding the ball, defender within 1 m, anywhere
5 s holding the ball in the frontcourt, defender within 6 ft
May be touched once it has touched the ring
2 in the 1st half, 3 in the 2nd (max 2 in the last 2 min of Q4), 1 per OT; 60 s
7 per game, max 4 in Q4 and 2 after the later of 3:00 or the 2nd mandatory; 2 per OT
Yes; from 2025-26 the Replay Center rules on proximate fouls in out-of-bounds challenges
Out of bounds, goaltending or basket interference, restricted area; needs a timeout (2025-26)
Out of bounds, backcourt, possession before a foul, foul charged to the correct player; no timeout needed (2025-26)

entries.definition: Moving the feet illegally while holding a live ball. After gaining control on the move or ending a dribble, a player may take two steps to stop, pass or shoot; to start a dribble, the ball must leave the hand before the second step. NBA also bans the "hop" (same foot twice) and sliding after falling with the ball.
Travel: jumping with the ball and landing still holding it.
Dribbling with two hands at once, or starting a second dribble after ending the first, unless a shot, an opponent's touch or a fumble came in between.
Dribble with the hand under the ball, or pausing it then continuing to dribble.
Offensive player stays in the lane more than 3 consecutive seconds while his team controls the ball in the frontcourt. Allowance while shooting or leaving.
NBA only: a defender may not stay in the lane more than 3 seconds unless actively guarding someone (arm's length, guarding stance). Penalty: technical foul.
FIBA: player holding the ball with a defender within 1 m must pass, shoot or dribble within 5 s. NCAA: frontcourt only, within 6 ft. NBA has no such rule.
NBA: below the free-throw line extended, a player may not dribble with his back or side to the basket for more than 5 s.
The thrower-in must release the ball within 5 s.
The offense must get the ball into the frontcourt within 8 s (FIBA, NBA) or 10 s (NCAA).

entries.aka: Over and back, ball returned to backcourt
entries.definition: The team in control in its frontcourt is first to touch the ball after it returns to the backcourt.
No shot that leaves the hand and touches the rim before the shot clock expires.
Touching a shot on its downward flight above the rim, or after it hits the backboard, while it can still score.

Touching the ball, ring, net or backboard in ways that affect a shot, such as reaching through from below or touching the ball inside the basket. NCAA (2025-26): putting a hand on the backboard or ring to gain an advantage is now basket interference, not a technical.
Deliberately striking the ball with the foot or leg. Accidental contact is not a violation.
The last player to touch the ball before it goes out loses possession.
Players from both teams have hands firmly on the ball and neither can gain control without roughness.
Referee tosses the ball between two opponents, at the start (all codes) and for held balls where the code still uses it.
FIBA and NCAA settle jump-ball situations by alternating throw-ins tracked by an arrow; the NBA still jumps.
Entering the lane early or other illegal acts during a free throw. Time to shoot: NBA 10 s, FIBA 5 s.
NBA: violation even without contact. FIBA: technical foul.
Technical foul (FIBA, NBA) unless to avoid injury.
Illegal contact with an opponent: holding, pushing, blocking, charging, tripping.
Foul on a player in the act of shooting: made shot counts plus 1 FT; missed 2 = 2 FTs; missed 3 = 3 FTs.
Basket scored while fouled, plus one free throw. A four-point play is the same on a made three.
Foul by a player on the team in control. No free throws; ball to the opponent.
Offensive player moves into a defender's torso after the defender set legal position.
Defender illegally impedes an opponent, usually by moving into his path or not being set.
Offensive foul by the ball handler; often loosely called a charge.
Foul while neither team controls the ball, such as on a rebound.
Each personal foul counts toward a team total that triggers the penalty.
Team-foul level after which non-shooting fouls give free throws (values in the table).
NCAA men: a second free throw only if the first goes in.
Informal NCAA men's term: 10+ team fouls in a half, so every foul gives two shots.
Two opponents foul each other at about the same time. Both charged, no free throws.
Non-contact foul for conduct or procedure: disrespect, delay, faking a foul, hanging on the rim.
NBA: unnecessary (F1) or unnecessary and excessive (F2) contact. Both: 2 FTs plus possession; F2 is an ejection, as are two F1s in a game.

FIBA (also NCAA women): contact not aimed at the ball, excessive contact, unnecessary contact to stop a fast break, or contact from behind or the side on a player breaking to the basket with no defender ahead.
FIBA: flagrantly unsportsmanlike action; immediate removal. Equivalent to the NBA's flagrant 2.
NBA: foul on a player with a clear path to the basket in transition. 2 FTs plus possession.
NBA: deliberate defensive foul away from the action in the last two minutes of any period, or any foul before a throw-in is released. 1 FT plus possession.
FIBA: defender fouls on court while the ball is out for a throw-in in the last 2 min of Q4 or OT. 1 FT plus possession.
NBA: a punch that connects. 2 FTs, possession, ejection and suspension.
Physical altercation; FIBA disqualifies bench members who leave the bench area.
Illegally using hands to slow or steer an opponent.
Removal on reaching the foul limit: FIBA 5, NBA 6, NCAA men 5. FIBA also disqualifies after 2 technicals, 2 unsportsmanlike, or one of each.
Exaggerated fall to sell a foul. FIBA (2024): first fake draws a warning even if a foul is also called; the second is a technical.
Each player owns the imaginary cylinder above his footprint (palms in front, buttocks behind, arms and legs at the sides). Entering an opponent's cylinder and causing contact is a foul.
A player who jumps straight up within his cylinder keeps his right to that space. Leaving it and causing contact makes him responsible.
Defender facing the opponent with both feet on the floor. Against the ball handler, time and distance do not apply.
FIBA: starts when the player begins moving the ball up toward the basket (on drives, when the ball comes to rest in the hands) and ends on release. NBA: starts at the gather on drives.
A basket counts if the shooting motion started before the foul. NCAA men (2025-26): a shooter fouled after ending the dribble may finish the pivot or step he is on.
Putting the ball in play from out of bounds.
NBA: where the ball was when the whistle blew; play resumes from there after a suspension.
FIBA (2024): referees can fix wrong free throws, points, fouls or clock errors only within set deadlines; shot-clock errors cannot be fixed after a change of possession.
Video review of listed situations (end-of-period shots, late-game goaltending, foul types, etc.).
Untimed finish: a target score is set and play continues until a team reaches it.
Half-court, three-a-side FIBA format (Olympic since 2021): 12-s shot clock, 10 min or first to 21, 1 and 2 points, ball must be cleared behind the arc after a change of possession.

sections.title: Stats and analytics
sections.note: Formulas are as published by Basketball-Reference and NBA.com. Possession-based stats exist because raw totals reward fast teams; per-100-possession numbers compare teams at any pace.

entries.definition: Any made (FG) or attempted (FGA) shot except free throws; FG% = FG / FGA.
Pass that leads directly to a teammate's basket.
Losing possession without a shot: bad pass, violation, offensive foul.
Points scored inside the painted area.
Point differential while a player or lineup is on the floor.
10 or more in two stat categories in one game.
10 or more in three categories. Quadruple- and quintuple-doubles extend the idea.
Uncredited rebound logged so that misses equal rebounds, for example after a missed first free throw.
Box score with one minute played and zeros elsewhere; coined by Harvey Pollack.
NBA.com: last 5 minutes of the 4th quarter or overtime with the score within 5 points.
One team's turn with the ball, ending with a score, miss rebounded by the defense, or turnover. An offensive rebound extends the same possession.
Estimated possessions per 48 minutes (Basketball-Reference uses 40 for the WNBA).
Points scored per 100 possessions (team), or points produced per 100 possessions (player, Basketball-Reference) / team points per 100 while on court (NBA.com).
Points allowed per 100 possessions.
Offensive rating minus defensive rating.
Points divided by possessions; Synergy counts turnovers and fouls in the denominator.
(FG + 0.5 × 3P) / FGA. Credits a three as worth 1.5 twos.
PTS / (2 × TSA), with TSA = FGA + 0.44 × FTA. Shooting efficiency including free throws.
Share of team plays a player ends while on court (shots, free throws that end a possession, turnovers).
Estimated share of teammates' field goals a player assisted while on court.
Assists per 100 possessions a player uses.
Turnovers per 100 plays: TOV / (FGA + 0.44 × FTA + TOV).
Share of available offensive, defensive or total rebounds a player or team grabbed.
Share of opponent possessions ending in the player's steal; share of opponent two-point attempts he blocked.
Free throws made per field-goal attempt (FT / FGA), as used in the Four Factors.
Dean Oliver's keys to winning, with his approximate weights: shooting (eFG%) 40%, turnovers (TOV%) 25%, rebounding (ORB%/DRB%) 20%, free throws (FT rate) 15%.
John Hollinger's per-minute all-in-one rating of a player's box-score production.
NBA.com share of all positive and negative box-score events in games a player plays; built to be comparable to PER.
Box-score estimate of points per 100 possessions a player adds over a league-average player.
BPM-based points per 100 team possessions above a replacement-level (-2.0) player, scaled to 82 games; × 2.70 converts to wins.
Estimated wins a player contributed; WS/48 is per 48 minutes, league average about 0.100.
European box-score rating: positive stats minus negative stats.
Ken Pomeroy's predictive NCAA men's ratings.
NCAA's ranking metric for tournament selection; replaced the RPI.
How much a player's shooting threat pulls defenders toward him even without the ball.
Screen that directly leads to a teammate's made field goal.
Pass to a player who records an assist within one second, without dribbling.
Pass to a teammate who shoots within one dribble of the catch.
Defender gets a hand on the ball on a non-shot.
Shot where a defender closes out with a hand up before release; tracking counts the nearest defender within 3.5 ft.
Offensive fouls drawn by a defender taking a charge.
Contact with an opponent chasing a rebound that clearly keeps him from it.
Times a player catches and possesses the ball.
Half-court attacks off the dribble toward the basket, excluding plays that start near the rim.
Opponents' FG% on shots the player defends.
One-on-one possessions, including broken actions where the handler stalls and then attacks.
Possessions before the defense is set; no shot-clock cutoff.
Ball handler finishes a ball-screen play with a pull-up, floater or rim attempt, including rejects. Passes out are tracked separately.
The screener's rolls, slips and pops.
Back-to-basket and face-up post possessions.
Catch without first running off a screen (standing, relocating), including attacking closeouts.
Dribble handoffs and flip or pitch plays.
Basket cuts, screen cuts (UCLA, flex) and flash cuts.
Player runs off an off-ball screen and shoots or attacks; UCLA and flex screens count as cuts.
Tip-ins and quick shots after offensive rebounds.
Catch-all: loose-ball shots, some inbounds plays, turnovers outside other actions.
Unblocked shot that misses both rim and backboard.
Ugly miss that clanks off the rim.
Shot that goes in without touching the rim.
Shot that hits the rim.
Shot that looks in but rims back out.
Shot that circles the rim before falling in or out.
Ball stuck on the ledge behind the rim.
Ball stuck between the rim and the backboard.
Late made shot that effectively ends the game.
An assist.
A rebound.
The ball.
A three-pointer.
Well beyond the three-point line.
A player starting to make most of his shots.
Time a jumper stays in the air.
Player who rarely passes.
Player who shoots far too often, often bad shots.
Off-balance, low-percentage shot.
Very low-probability shot, usually a long three.
High-arcing made shot.
Having your shot blocked.
Defender positioning early in anticipation of a play.
Player who rarely gets off the bench.
Zero points despite real minutes.
A 55-point game.
Single digits in points, rebounds and assists; popularized by Charles Barkley about Draymond Green.
"Did not play, coach's decision": healthy but unused.
U.S. spring and summer club basketball paid for by families.
College player expected to go to the NBA draft after one season.
Drafting an overseas player who stays abroad for now.
The line between teams likely in or out of a postseason tournament.
Long-shot team that wins its conference tournament, taking a bid from a bubble team.
The fast-break Lakers of 1979-1991 (Magic Johnson, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar; Pat Riley from 1981-82), and the glamour around them.
Chuck Daly's late-1980s Pistons plan to slow Michael Jordan with physical play and shifting double teams.
Warriors small-ball unit, 2014-2019: Curry, Thompson, Iguodala, Draymond Green at center, plus Harrison Barnes, then Kevin Durant from 2016-17.

sections.title: Disputed and multi-meaning terms
sections.note: These are the terms most likely to cause confusion in an app or a coaching session. Where sources disagree, both versions are given; nothing here is settled by guesswork.

groups.note: Conflicts settled by the rulebook. NBA.com's 2024 explainer says a FIBA technical gives one free throw and possession at center court; FIBA 2024 Art. 36.3.2 says play resumes with the team that had the ball, from where it stopped. A 2025 Basketball for Coaches article says NBA unsportsmanlike technicals give two free throws and possession; NBA Rule 12 says one free throw per technical. This lexicon follows the rulebooks in both cases.

entries.definition: FIBA: the painted lane (Art. 2.5.3). NBA and NCAA: the 4-ft arc under the basket. FIBA's arc is the "no-charge semicircle".
(1) A blocked shot. (2) A blocking foul. (3) The low-block spot beside the lane.
(1) The half of the court attacked or defended. (2) A team's forwards and center, or its guards.
(1) The corner of the free-throw line and lane. (2) An illegal elbow swing.
(1) Floor area at the free-throw line extended. (2) A 2 or 3 who plays there.
Most sources: the same action, a pin-down into a dribble handoff. The Action Dictionary index uses Zoom more broadly for any screen-plus-DHO combo.
(1) Early-offense wing action: pass-and-follow handoff or wing ball screen. (2) Triangle-offense name for Chicago. (3) The "21" 5-out alignment.
The weak-side screen is called a back screen (Grantland, Breakthrough) or a flare (Action Dictionary). The action is the same: baseline drive, shooter freed to the far corner.
Coaching sources: any screen sending a cutter toward the rim. Wikipedia: a post player screening for a perimeter teammate.
(1) Pass, then receive a handoff back. (2) "Elbow get": a big-to-big ball screen at the elbow.
(1) Changing the angle of a ball screen at the last moment. (2) A pass followed by a handoff or pitch back.
(1) Going over a ball screen (coverage). (2) Action Dictionary alias for a dribble handoff. (3) Alias for the Iverson cut.
(1) Going under a ball screen (coverage). (2) Action Dictionary alias for the inverted pick-and-roll.
Action Dictionary lists several: a back screen that hooks into an elbow screen, a middle ball-screen call, or a brush cut.
(1) Baseline inbounds alignment. (2) "Stack pick-and-roll" = Spain. (3) Low stack set. (4) Coach's Clipboard calls the 1-4 high set the "stack offense".
Widely used phrase, but neither FIBA nor NBA rule text uses it; both count steps from the first foot down after gaining control.
"Charge" is often used for any offensive foul by the ball handler; the rule term in some codes is player-control foul.
FIBA's disqualifying foul matches the NBA's flagrant 2; FIBA's unsportsmanlike foul has its own criteria (including fast-break fouls) and does not map one-to-one onto flagrant 1.
Called the "10-second line" where the backcourt count is 10 s (NCAA, U.S. high school); FIBA and the NBA count 8 s.
About 16 ft from the rim (SI, Basketball for Coaches) versus about 2 ft inside the three-point line (Wikipedia).
Breakthrough: Jerry Tarkanian's UNLV. Wikipedia: created by Pitt assistant Fran Webster (1970s) and brought to UNLV by Tim Grgurich.
Coach's Clipboard: introduced by Spain's national team. Hooper University: Sergio Scariolo, heavily used at the 2016 Olympics. Compatible, but only one names a coach and year.
